title: Why you can't make money charging $1 per month: price higher, move upmarket
summary: Rob explains why a $1/month SaaS price point is a trap: it demands thousands of customers, heavy support, and free-only acquisition channels. He recommends pricing at $50-$100+/month, selling to businesses, and using "Aspirational Pricing" to add value instead of cutting price.

principles.text: Very low prices create unsustainable math: you need thousands of customers to earn a small income.
principles.quote: If your goal is a meager $2k per month you need 2k customers.

principles.text: Low price points rule out paid acquisition because CAC outruns LTV, forcing reliance on SEO, word of mouth and virality.
principles.quote: at $1/mo (or $7/mo), you won’t have the budget to run ads. The cost to acquire each customer (CAC) will be too high compared to the lifetime value (LTV) you will receive from each one.

principles.text: Counterintuitively, cheaper products attract worse customers: more churn, more support, more price sensitivity.
principles.quote: lower priced products tend to have higher churn, higher support burdens, and more price-sensitive customers.

principles.text: Move upmarket and sell to businesses rather than consumers to build a larger SaaS.
principles.quote: I have personally moved each successive product upmarket, and moved to selling to businesses.

principles.text: Aspirational Pricing: when customers push back on price, build what makes your current price worth it rather than lowering it.
principles.quote: when people ask you to lower your price, you ask “What would I need to build to make it worth the price I’m charging today?” And then build those features

principles.text: Charge $50-$100/month or more; if stuck at low prices, bill annually to get cash up-front to reinvest.
principles.quote: Charging $50 or $100/month (or more) is such a better way to go, in my experience with my own companies and those I advise.
